properties.occurrenceRemarks: Sunda Colugo (Galeopterus variegatus) is a nocturnal, arboreal mammal also known as a colugo or “flying lemur” of Southeast Asia. It has a skin membrane (patagium) extending from the neck to the forelimbs, hind limbs, and tail, enabling it to glide between trees over distances of tens of meters. Active at night, it feeds on leaves, flowers, and fruits, and plays an important ecological role as an arboreal herbivore. During the day, it typically rests clinging to tree trunks, using its brownish-gray coloration for camouflage.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: The Bantimurung Bulusaraung Biosphere Reserve lies in southern Sulawesi, Indonesia, and comprises three main landscapes: Bantimurung, Bulusaraung and Maros–Pangkep. The Maros–Pangkep karst is among the largest tower-karst systems in the region. Within the core area, Bantimurung Bulusaraung National Park is internationally known for its butterflies, with more than 250 recorded species. Communities such as the Makassar and Bugis have maintained their traditions for centuries. While nature- and culture-based tourism are well developed, agriculture, including paddy farming, dryland cultivation, livestock and fishing, remains the main livelihood.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve extends from flat and undulating plains to hilly and mountainous terrain, rising to around 1,565 m in the north-east. Hilly tracts include intrusive, sedimentary and karst ridges, with low-relief plains between tower-karst outcrops. The Maros–Pangkep Karst covers around 40,000 ha, and is one of Indonesia’s few tower-karst landscapes; its extensive caves, rich in stalactites and stalagmites, contrast with the country’s more widespread hill karst. Karst caves host obligate cave-dwelling fauna such as dim-eyed and blind fish (Bostrychus), blind cockroaches (Nocticola), the beetle Eustra saripaensis, cave crickets (Rhaphidophora) and cave mites (Trombidiidae). Three principal forest ecosystems occur supporting high biodiversity: forest on karst (over limestone), lowland forest and lower montane forest. About 710 plant species are recorded, including wanga palm (Pigafetta filaris), sugar palms (Arenga) and protected Sulawesi ebony (Diospyros celebica). The reserve’s forests provide essential ecosystem services, from carbon storage and local climate regulation to flood mitigation and water purification. Bantimurung Bulusaraung National Park, within the core area, is internationally renowned for butterflies: more than 250 species are recorded, including the endemics Papilio blumei and Papilio gigon, and the protected Troides haliphron and Cethosia myrina.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: The Bromo Tengger Semeru-Arjuno Biosphere Reserve is located in the province of East Java and encompasses an active volcano, Mount Bromo at 2,392 m above sea level. There are 1,025 reported species of flora, of which 226 species are orchids and 260 are medicinal and ornamental plants. Plant families commonly found in this area include Fagaceae, Moraceae and Anacardiaceae. Some of the mammal species found in the core area are included in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Livestock farming of cattle, goats, sheep, horses, rabbits and chickens contributes to the local economy. The main economic activity is tourism.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The Bromo Tengger Semeru-Arjuno Biosphere Reserve is located on Java Island in East Java and forms part of the Indo-Malayan region. The biosphere reserve lies in a mountainous area that includes the active volcano Mount Bromo at 2,392 m above sea level, as well as Tengger Semeru, Arjuno and Mount Welirang. The core area incorporates mountains with an altitude of over 1,000 m above sea level that are covered with tropical rainforest. Several types of terrestrial ecosystem are found in the reserve, including cultivated areas, secondary forest and primary forest. The primary forest includes lowland rainforest, mountain rainforest, desert, savannah and sub-alpine ecosystems. In addition, the reserve incorporates lakes, and aquatic and riparian ecosystems. The reserve is home to about 1,025 species of flora, including 226 species of the Orchidaceae family and 260 species recorded as traditional medicinal plants and ornamentals. An inventory of fauna recorded 158 species, consisting of 22 mammal species, of which 15 are protected, 130 bird species, of which 27 are protected, and six species of reptiles. Protected mammal species include the Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica), leopard (Panthera pardus), Malayan porcupine (Hystrix brachyura) and Indian muntjac (Muntiacus muntjak). Protected bird species include the Brahminy kite (Haliastur indus), spotted kestrel (Falco moluccensis), green peafowl (Pavo muticus), Javan kingfisher (Halcyon cyanoventris) and Sunda minivet (Pericrocotus miniatus).

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: The Karimunjawa-Jepara-Muria Biosphere Reserve in Central Java, Indonesia, is located in the mountainous region surrounding Mount Muria. It is critical in preserving the biodiversity of the central region on the island of Java. It includes a large variety of ecosystems, including small islands and marine ecosystems, as well as lowland and mountain tropical rainforests.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Karimunjawa-Jepara-Muria’s core area is situated in its islands. The diverse marine ecosystem hosts about 69 hard corals and 15 sea cucumber species. Karimunjawa National Park is home to numerous nesting sites for sea turtles, including the hawksbill and green turtle. Marine species, from giant clams (known locally as kima) to bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus), are protected by law, helping to maintain a healthy marine biota. The lowland and mountain tropical rainforests range from sea level to 1,500 metres above sea level. These forests support a variety of life, with over 130 bird species recorded. The biosphere reserve surrounds Mount Muria, a dormant volcano. The Javan deer (Cervus timorensis) occurs in the forests and is protected by law.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Wakatobi is an acronym for the four main islands of Wangi-Wangi, Kaledupa, Tomia and Binongko, which together with smaller islands comprise the Tukang Besi Archipelago at the south-eastern tip of Sulawesi. The archipelago is renowned for the diversity of its coral gardens. Wakatobi’s 3.4 million acres of islands and waters were declared a national park in 1996. The ethnically diverse human population aims to make the area a learning laboratory in fields such as fisheries and agriculture.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Wakatobi has diverse ecosystems with many marine and coastal species of seagrass, coral reefs, fish used both for consumption and for sale, seabirds, turtles, cetaceans and mangroves. There are about 590 fish species, 396 coral reef species, 22 major and 11 associate mangrove species, and 9 of the 12 seagrass species found in Indonesia. Rare and endangered species with protected status include the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), green turtle (Chelonia mydas), napoleon fish (Cheilinus undulatus), canary crab (Birgus latro), giant clams (Tridacna), trochus (Trochus niloticus), dugong (Dugong dugon), and dolphins including Delphinus delphis, Stenella longirostris and Tursiops truncatus. There are 85 marine bird species in Wakatobi, for example brown booby (Sula leucogaster plotus), Malaysian plover (Charadrius peronii) and common kingfisher (Alcedo atthis). Several cetacean species are also found in the area, including sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus), short-finned pilot whale (Globicephala macrorhynchus), killer whale (Orcinus orca), pygmy killer whale (Feresa attenuata), pantropical spotted dolphin (Stenella attenuata), rough-toothed dolphin (Steno bredanensis), Risso’s dolphin (Grampus griseus), bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) and melon-headed whale (Peponocephala electra).

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Located in the westernmost part of Papua, Indonesia, the Raja Ampat Biosphere Reserve spans across roughly 610 islands, atolls, and takas, of which only 34 are inhabited. This vast archipelago lies at the heart of the Coral Triangle, one of the planet’s most important marine biodiversity hotspots. Its landscapes and seascapes combine mangroves, white and black sand beaches, rainforests, and some of the richest coral reefs on Earth, forming a globally significant socio-ecological mosaic.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The marine environment of Raja Ampat covers ten core marine areas. Terrestrial habitats include lowland and montane rainforests as well as protected wildlife reserves. The reefs host over 75% of all known coral species, more than 1,320 species of coral reef fish, and five rare or endangered species of sea turtles, including the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata). Around 60% of coral reefs are in good to excellent condition, and the region supports mangrove forests, seagrass meadows, deep reef systems, and unique coastal ecosystems that together underpin one of the highest concentrations of marine biodiversity on Earth.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: The Belambangan Biosphere Reserve is located in East Java Province and incorporates three national parks, Alas Purwo, Baluran and Meru, and one nature reserve, Kawah Ijen. The reserve comprises terrestrial and marine ecosystems featuring karst landscapes and savannah. It includes different forest types, notably alpine and subalpine, upper, dry and lower montane, lowland, coastal and mangrove. The site also features seagrass beds and coral reefs. The main economic activities are agriculture and horticulture, as well as agroforestry, notably teak and mahogany.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The Belambangan Biosphere Reserve is in East Java Province on Java Island and forms part of the Indo-Malayan region. It lies within Banyuwangi Regency, Situbondo, Bondowoso Regency and Jember Regency in East Java, and includes the mountain areas of Ijen and Mount Raung. The core area is covered with tropical rainforest at altitudes from 0 to 1,000 m above sea level. The reserve includes both terrestrial and marine ecosystems such as karst landscapes, savannah, alpine and subalpine forest, montane forest, lowland bamboo forest, coastal forest and seagrass beds. Mangroves are also present, and coral reef ecosystems are found in the buffer zone. More than 300 fish species have been identified. The reefs are dominated by coral species of the genus Acropora. The region is a biodiversity hotspot with many faunal species, including the banteng or Javanese wild bull (Bos javanicus), Christmas frigatebird (Fregata andrewsi), green peafowl (Pavo muticus) and the endangered Javan leopard (Panthera pardus). In addition, four species of sea turtle nest on the south and east coast of Alas Purwo National Park: olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea), leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea), hawksbill (Eretmochelys imbricata) and green turtle (Chelonia mydas).

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Bukit Batu is a peatland area in Sumatra that features sustainable timber production and two wildlife reserves. These reserves are home to the Sumatran tiger, elephant, tapir and sun bear. Research activities in the biosphere reserve include the monitoring of flagship species and in-depth study of peatland ecology. Initial studies indicate good potential for sustainable economic development that uses flora and fauna to support inhabitants’ economic welfare.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Recognised as part of the Sumatra peat swamp ecoregion, Giam Siak Kecil–Bukit Batu has a unique habitat and plays a significant role in sustaining populations of rare, endangered and endemic species. About 189 plant species, from 113 families and 59 genera, are recorded in this area. Twenty-nine of these plant species are categorised as protected under CITES Appendices I and III. Nine protected species recorded in this area include: red costulata (family Apocynaceae); nyatoh (Ganua motleyana), family Sapotaceae; tiger orchid (Grammatophyllum speciosum), family Orchidaceae; daaropara (Knema), family Myristicaceae; mengris (Kompassia malaccensis), family Mimosaceae; pitcher plants (Nepenthes), family Nepenthaceae; suntai (Palaquium leiocarpum), family Sapotaceae; and balam (Palaquium burckii), family Sapotaceae. The core area is dominated by peat swamp forest. Recorded plant species here include ramin (Gonystylus bancanus), nyatoh (Palaquium leiocarpum), durian burung (Durio carinatus), meranti bunga (Shorea teysmanniana) and punak (Tetramerista glabra). Several key animal species are recorded in the core area and are listed as protected and endangered under CITES Appendix I. biosphere_reserves.description:

Research activities in the biosphere reserve include the monitoring of flagship species and in-depth study of peatland ecology. biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Situated between Flores and Sumbawa in Indonesia, the Komodo Biosphere Reserve and National Park is renowned for its population of about 5,000 giant lizards, also called Komodo dragons (Varanus komodoensis). They exist nowhere else in the world and are of significant interest to scientists studying the theory of evolution. In addition to Komodo Island, the biosphere reserve encompasses the islands of Rinca and Padar, as well as numerous islets. It also includes one of the world’s richest marine environments with coral reefs.

Komodo has one of the world’s richest marine environments. It includes more than 260 species of reef-building coral, 70 species of sponge, ascidians, marine worms, molluscs, echinoderms and crustaceans, as well as cartilaginous fishes and more than 1,000 species of bony fishes. Marine reptiles include green turtle and hawksbill turtle, and marine mammals include dolphins, whales and dugongs. Notable species of high commercial value include sea cucumbers, Napoleon wrasse (Cheilinus undulatus) and groupers. biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Located in Central Java in the Indo-Malayan region, the biosphere reserve spans 254,877 ha. It is home to Gunung Merapi National Park, Gunung Merbabu National Park and Sermo Wildlife Reserve, each critical in protecting various endemic Javanese species. The Java–Bali montane forest type at the site protects the biodiversity of the Indo-Malayan region, as well as a limestone formation in the Menoreh area.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The tropical forest of the Merapi Merbabu Menoreh Biosphere Reserve is part of the Java–Bali montane forest type. It plays an important role in biodiversity conservation in the Sundaland region, as well as in conserving limestone (karst) formations in the Menoreh part of the reserve. The core areas are dominated by montane forest and karst and are recognised as supporting a significant water reservoir that supplies the buffer zone and transition area. They also play an important role in controlling floods. These core areas harbour several protected, threatened and endemic flora and fauna. At least 48 species are recorded across these categories: nine mammals, 35 birds, two fish, one amphibian and one insect. Notable examples include the long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), the leopard (Panthera pardus) and the black-winged starling (Acridotheres melanopterus).

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: The biosphere includes Lombok Island, part of the Lesser Sunda Islands. It consists of relatively flat coastal areas and hilly and mountainous areas. The highest peak is Mount Rinjani, the second-highest volcanic mountain in Indonesia at 3,726 metres above sea level. The area has a very high level of biodiversity, comprising various types of forest vegetation, including savannah forest and mountain and lowland rain forest, about 40 per cent of which are primary forests. The inhabitants’ main sources of revenue come from horticulture such as vegetables and fruits, cereal crops such as rice, animal husbandry including cows, goats and chickens, and the cultivation of coffee and cacao.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The biosphere reserve is a lowland area extending from the coast to hilly and mountainous terrain, with elevations ranging from 0 m to 3,726 m above sea level. Slopes are classified as gentle at 0–15 per cent, moderate at 15–25 per cent, sloping at 25–40 per cent, and steep at more than 40 per cent. A relatively sloping area located in the south and north-east lies at an altitude of 0–1,500 m above sea level at the foothill of Mount Rinjani. The highest peak is Mount Rinjani at 3,726 m above sea level. Adjacent mountains are separated by vast valleys and deep ravines, with steep and rocky slopes. In the western valley of Mount Rinjani lies Segara Anak Lake at 2,100 m above sea level, with waters rich in sulphur. In the middle of Segara Anak Lake, the “new volcano” called Mount Barujari at 2,376 m has risen. The volcano is still active, and the last eruption occurred in 2009. The reserve is a habitat for various important flora and fauna species of the Lesser Sunda and many other species adapted to the unique mountain tropical ecosystem of Lombok Island. The core area houses at least 19 species of mammals, 8 species of reptiles, 5 species of amphibians, 154 species of birds, 20 insect species, 447 species of trees, 59 species of ferns, 117 species of mushrooms, 55 species of orchids, 28 species of lianas and 6 species of rattans.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Saleh–Moyo–Tambora (SAMOTA) comprises five major ecosystems: small islands; a coastal area of mangrove; coastal, lowland and mountain forests; and savannah. Its core area plays an important role in conserving the region’s biodiversity. The buffer zone and transition area have agricultural potential for the production of fruit and vegetables, as well as rice, coffee and cacao, and for animal husbandry. The beauty of the Tambora Mountains has tourist potential, while Sumba Island communities attract cultural tourism.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The three areas that comprise the Biosphere Reserve feature a great deal of biological diversity. In Saleh Bay, for instance, dugong species can be found in the mangrove habitat, as well as dolphins. In Moyo, there are 30 bird species, nine of which are protected. These include small crested yellow cockatoos (Cacatua sulphurea), orange-footed scrubfowl (Megapodius reinwardt), horned cikukua (Philemon boceroides), honey sriganti (Nectarinia jugularis), elegant pitta (Pitta elegans), parrots (Gracula religiosa), Halcyon chloris, Haliastur indus. In addition to various species of birds in Moyo and Satonda Island, there are several other species of animals such as timor deer (Cervus timorensis), wild boar (Sus), Macaca fasicularis and reticulated python (Python reticulatus). The Tambora National Park area has a high diversity of plant species. Vegetation is distributed across three forest ecosystem types, ranging from seasonal forests to tropical rainforests and savannah forests. Dense vegetation cover forms a solid ecosystem, giving the Tambora National Park region a strategic role as a life-support system to ensure the continuity of ecological functions in the region.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Located on the south-east coast of Sumatra, this biosphere reserve includes Berbak and Sembilang National Parks as well as two wildlife reserves. It contains undisturbed swamp-forest peat ecosystems, freshwater swamp forests and mangroves, and lowland forests surrounding riverbanks, with swamps reaching depths of up to 10 metres. Palm oil plantations, rubber, traditional agriculture, including rice and dry fields, and timber are the main economic activities.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The topography of the biosphere reserve is varied. While most of the land is flat, some is sloping (0–20 per cent), with an altitude of 0–140 m above sea level. The most typical topographic features are tree-dominated wetlands, including freshwater swamp forests, seasonally flooded forests and wooded swamps on inorganic soils, permanent freshwater lakes, such as large oxbow lakes, and intertidal forested wetlands with mangrove swamps, nipah swamps and tidal freshwater swamp forests. Permanent rivers, streams and creeks occur throughout the site. There are forested peatlands and peat swamp forests, man-made wetland areas, and lowland rainforest areas. With high biodiversity, the area is a suitable habitat for various flora and fauna of Sumatra as well as rare species. There are 23 palm species (Arecaceae), 250 bird species (including 22 migratory wader species), 13 reptile species, 60,000 ha of freshwater swamp and 1,500 ha of mangrove forest recorded. A large alluvial delta in the area serves as one of the most important habitats for migratory birds in the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, whose total number is about 0.5–1 million. Several protected species include Sumatran tiger (Panthera tigris sumatrae), Malayan tapir (Tapirus indicus), Malayan sun bear (Helarctos malayanus), saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), marble cat (Pardofelis marmorata) and leaf monkey (Presbytis rubicunda).

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Situated in West Java Province to the south of Jakarta, the Cibodas Biosphere Reserve exemplifies a humid tropical ecosystem under strong human pressure. The Gunung Gede–Pangrango National Park constitutes the core area and encompasses twin volcanoes and mountainous rainforests, including many species endemic to Java. The buffer zone comprises production forests, tea plantations and horticultural fields. The majority of the transition area is covered by irrigated rice fields and human settlements.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area consists of twin volcanoes: Mount Gede (2,958 m) and Mount Pangrango (3,109 m). A high saddle known as Kandang Badak, at 2,400 m above sea level, connects the two summits. The mountain slopes are very steep and are cut by rapidly flowing streams that carve deep valleys and long ridges. Generally, the core area is well drained. A few naturally occurring swamps, including Rawa Goyonggong, Rawa Denok and Situgunung, enrich the variety of habitats. Based on elevation and forest stratification, the vegetation is characterised by three ecosystem types: sub-montane, below 1,500 m above sea level; montane, 1,500–2,400 m; and sub-alpine, above 2,400 m. biosphere_reserves.title_en: Betung Kerihun Danau Sentarum Kapuas Hulu
biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Located at the eastern tip of Kalimantan Barat Province on the island of Borneo, the biosphere reserve consists of the two national parks of Betung Kerihun and Danau Sentarum. It features unique lowland and montane tropical rainforests that are home to a great diversity of flora and fauna.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Betung Kerihun–Danau Sentarum Kapuas Hulu Biosphere Reserve is an area now experiencing continual erosion. It includes lowlands and basins, as well as lakes and swampy plains. In the highlands there are many narrow, elongated swamps surrounded by small hills. These swamps are continually inundated with water, especially during periods of heavy rainfall. The highlands are situated at higher elevations. There are 1,216 species of flora identified in Betung Kerihun National Park, comprising 418 genera and 110 families. Seventy-five species are endemic to Borneo, and 14 species were newly recorded. Faunal diversity is also very high, including 48 species of mammals, 17 species of primates, 301 species of birds, 103 species of herpetofauna, 112 species of fish and 170 species of insects. Danau Sentarum National Park is a habitat for approximately 794 species of trees and shrubs, orchids, about 147 species of mammals, 67 species of reptiles, 22 species of Indonesian amphibians, 311 species of birds and 266 species of fish.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: The Bunaken Tangkoko Minahasa Biosphere Reserve in North Sulawesi is located in the heart of the Coral Triangle of the Indo-Pacific region in Indonesia. The biosphere reserve spans a total of 746,405.92 ha of terrestrial and marine habitats. The area encompasses a mosaic of ecological systems, including a coastal area with coral reefs and seagrass, mangrove and coastal forests, islands and terrestrial ecosystems. The biosphere reserve is home to over 130 species of mammals, including the Dian’s tarsier. The region profits from the production of cocoa, coffee, fisheries and ecotourism.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The core area of the Bunaken Tangkoko Minahasa Biosphere Reserve consists of five conservation areas: Bunaken Island National Park, Tangkoko Duasudara Nature Reserve, Batu Putih Nature Reserve, Gunung Lokon Nature Reserve, Manembe-Nembe Wildlife Reserve and Gunung Tumpa Forest Park. Bunaken National Marine Park represents Indonesia’s tropical sea ecosystem and is located at the centre of the marine and coastal biodiversity of the Indo-Pacific region. Mangroves in the Bunaken Island National Park are mostly located along the coasts of the small islands and Bunaken Island, where 34–46 mangrove species can be found, including Ceriops tagal, Rhizophora apiculata, Rhizophora mucronata, Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, Avicennia marina, Xylocarpus moluccensis, Sonneratia alba and Sonneratia caseolaris. Penyu hijau (Chelonia mydas) and Penyu sisik (Eretmochelys imbricata) are often seen when diving or snorkelling on reefs in the Bunaken National Park area. Mount Tumpa, one of the mountains in North Sulawesi Province, has a rich flora and fauna, including soil insects. It is a primary forest that is still intact and only slightly disturbed by human exploitation. Mount Lokon Nature Reserve has the unique ecosystem of the Mount Lokon area in the form of an active volcano area. It features mountain forests with active volcanoes and has two interesting caves. Primates found in this area are the Sulawesi black monkey or yaki (Macaca nigra), with a density of about two individuals per square kilometre, and the species of tangkasi (Tarsius spectrum). biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: This biosphere reserve and national park cover a vast area of tropical rainforest in northern Sumatra. Ecosystems include lowland evergreen dipterocarp forest, lower and upper montane rainforest, peat swamp forest, forest over limestone, sub-alpine meadows and heathlands, freshwater lakes and rivers, and sulphur mineral pools.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Gunung Leuser National Park is a rich yet vulnerable natural laboratory. According to MacKinnon and MacKinnon (1986), Gunung Leuser has the highest score for its conservation contribution to the Indo-Malaya conservation area. Leuser provides habitat for a wide range of fauna, including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish and invertebrates. It has an extensive list of bird species, up to 380 species. Gunung Leuser is also home to 36 of 50 Sundaland endemic bird species. Almost 65 per cent of the 129 mammal species in Sumatra are recorded in this area. The ecosystem provides habitat for key fauna such as the Sumatran elephant (Elephas maximus sumatranus), tiger (Panthera tigris sumatrae), rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatrensis) and orang-utan (Pongo abelii). The park is also habitat to the owa (lar gibbon, Hylobates lar) and the kedih (Presbytis thomasi). There are more than 4,000 plant species found in the park, including three of the 15 parasitic Rafflesia species. It is also a habitat for many medicinal plants (Brimacombe and Elliot, 1996). As a natural laboratory, Gunung Leuser is important for conservation, education, scientific research for local and foreign researchers, and ecotourism. The Orangutan Research Station in Ketambe, Southeast Aceh District, opened by Dr Herman D. Rijksen, remains an important site for researchers.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Lore Lindu Biosphere Reserve and National Park comprise one of the largest remaining mountainous rainforests of Sulawesi. It is of high importance for biodiversity, culture and archaeology. Approximately 90 per cent of the area is montane forest above 1,000 m in altitude, representing most of Sulawesi’s unique mountain flora and fauna.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Lore Lindu National Park is one of Sulawesi’s important nature reserves and is home to a wide variety of flora and fauna. The park is located about 60 km south of Palu. It covers a large area that includes lowland and highland mountain forests, dense forests, flat fertile valleys, rivers, lakes and hot springs. The total area is 217,991.18 ha, with altitudes ranging from 200 to 2,610 m above sea level. The park, with its beautiful scenery, holds a great number of endemic flora and fauna. It lies within Wallacea, a transitional zone between Asia and Australia. The park also serves as a water reservoir for three main rivers in Central Sulawesi: the Lariang, Gumbasa and Palu. The rugged interior of the park is home to Sulawesi’s largest native animals, such as anoas, babirusas, tarsiers, Tonkean macaques, marsupials and Sulawesi’s largest carnivorous mammal, the civet. The park is home to at least five species of squirrels, and 31 of its 38 rat species are endemic. There are at least 55 species of bats and 267 species of birds, including maleo birds and red-knobbed hornbills. Thousands of interesting insect species can be seen around the park, including butterflies, which can be seen flying along the watercourse or drinking from puddles and mudbanks.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Siberut is the largest of the four Mentawai Islands situated off the west coast of Sumatra. It has been isolated from the Sumatra mainland and the Sunda Shelf for at least 500,000 years, resulting in an exceptionally high degree of endemism. Sixty-five per cent of the animals are thought to be endemic. Lowland dipterocarp rainforest is the principal ecosystem.
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: Siberut Island is isolated from the mainland Sunda Shelf by the Mentawai Strait, about 155 km from Padang, the capital city of West Sumatra Province. It covers five ecosystem types: primary dipterocarp forest, mixed primary forest, swamp forest, coastal forest and mangrove forest. The forest area is still relatively natural, with large trees. Sixty-five per cent of mammal species and fifteen per cent of fauna on Siberut are endemic at some taxonomic level, making the island, with its limited surface, unique in the world. Four primate species are found only in this reserve: the Kloss gibbon, also called the dwarf siamang (Hylobates klossii), the Mentawai macaque (Macaca pagensis), the Mentawaian leaf monkey (Presbytis potenziani siberu) and the pig-tailed snub-nosed monkey (Nasalis concolor siberu). About 134 bird species are found on Siberut, of which 19 are endemic. More than 31 mammal species and 864 plant species are also recorded in the park.

biosphere_reserves.introduction_en: Taka Bonerate–Kepulauan Selayar Biosphere Reserve is located in the south of Sulawesi, in South Sulawesi Province (Selayar Islands Regency). It covers a large marine area with small islands, numerous fringing reefs and atolls. Mangrove forests act as a barrier against strong sea waves and provide shelter and spawning grounds for various fish, as well as habitat for fauna such as birds. The mangroves include 22–26 species from 14 families, including Rhizophora stylosa and Ceriops tagal. Protected and threatened animals found at the site include softshell turtles (family Trionychidae), the green turtle (Chelonia mydas) and the napoleon fish (Cheilinus undulatus).
biosphere_reserves.ecological_characteristics_en: The reserve lies between the Flores Sea, Java Sea and Banda Sea. It hosts the largest atoll in Southeast Asia and the third largest in the world. Coral reefs, mangroves, lagoons, sand dunes and seagrass are the main habitats. Coral reefs cover 91,382 ha and are a principal habitat for several species. Reef types found on the islands include atoll reefs (terumbu karang cincin), fringing reefs (terumbu karang tepi), barrier reefs (terumbu karang penghalang) and patch reefs (karang gosong). The reserve has high biodiversity, including several protected marine species such as the hawksbill turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), green turtle (Chelonia mydas), common dolphin (Delphinus delphis), napoleon fish (Cheilinus undulatus), sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) and short-finned pilot whale (Globicephala macrorhynchus). Between 22 and 26 mangrove species, belonging to 14 families, have been recorded. There are also 34 bird species: 12 land birds, 13 shorebirds and 9 seabirds.
